questions.stem: Which list gives the eight planets in order, starting nearest the Sun?
options: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Saturn, Jupiter, Uranus, Neptune
Venus, Mercury, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune, Uranus
Mercury, Venus, Mars, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
questions.explanation: From the Sun outwards the order is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. A common slip is swapping Jupiter and Saturn — Jupiter, the biggest planet, comes first, straight after the asteroid belt.

questions.stem: Which is the largest planet in the solar system?
options: Neptune
Uranus
Jupiter
Saturn
questions.explanation: Jupiter is the largest planet, with a diameter about 11 times Earth's and a giant storm called the Great Red Spot. Saturn is the second largest; its wide rings can make it look bigger than it is.

questions.stem: Venus is further from the Sun than Mercury, yet Venus has the hotter surface. Why?
options: Its iron core is far hotter than the core of any other planet
It spins very fast, so friction with its thick air heats the whole surface
Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat by the greenhouse effect
It is actually closer to the Sun than Mercury for most of each year
questions.explanation: Venus's dense carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat so strongly that its surface is about 460 °C, hotter than Mercury's. Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so heat escapes and its night side becomes extremely cold. Venus is never closer to the Sun than Mercury, and it actually spins very slowly.

questions.stem: Why does Mars look red?
options: Its surface is hot enough to glow a dull red
Its oceans reflect only red light from the Sun
Its thick atmosphere is made of a red gas
Its surface dust contains iron oxide, or rust
questions.explanation: Mars is covered in dust rich in iron oxide, the same compound as rust, which gives it a red-orange colour. Mars is cold, not hot enough to glow, has no oceans today and has only a very thin atmosphere.

questions.stem: How do the four inner planets differ from the four outer planets?
options: Inner planets each have many moons; outer planets have no moons at all
Inner planets are small and rocky; outer planets are giants of gas and ice
Inner planets are giants of gas and ice; outer planets are small and rocky
Inner planets all have ring systems; outer planets have no rings at all
questions.explanation: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are small rocky planets, while Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants and Uranus and Neptune are ice giants. The outer planets are the ones with rings and dozens of moons — Mercury and Venus have no moons at all.

questions.stem: Which planet is famous for its wide, bright system of rings?
options: Mars
Mercury
Venus
Saturn
questions.explanation: Saturn's rings are made of countless pieces of ice and rock and are easily seen through a small telescope. The other giant planets have only thin, faint rings, and rocky planets such as Mars, Mercury and Venus have none.

questions.stem: Which planet is tilted so far that it spins almost on its side as it orbits the Sun?
options: Mars
Uranus
Neptune
Saturn
questions.explanation: Uranus's axis is tilted by about 98°, so it rolls around its orbit almost on its side, giving each pole decades of continuous daylight followed by decades of darkness. Neptune, its near-twin in size and make-up, is tilted by only about 28°, similar to Earth and Mars.

questions.stem: In 2006 Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet. Which reason did astronomers give?
options: It was found to orbit Neptune rather than the Sun itself
It has not cleared other objects from the region around its orbit
It was found to have no moons orbiting it, unlike the real planets
It was found to be made of gas rather than rock and ice
questions.explanation: A planet must orbit the Sun, be massive enough to be rounded by its own gravity, and have cleared its orbit of other objects. Pluto meets the first two but shares its region with many other icy bodies. It has five known moons, the largest being Charon, so lacking moons was not the reason.

questions.stem: Where is the main asteroid belt?
options: Between Jupiter and Saturn
Between Mars and Jupiter
Between Earth and Mars
Between Venus and Earth
questions.explanation: The main asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter and contains millions of rocky objects. It divides the inner rocky planets from the outer giant planets, which is a handy way to remember where it sits.

questions.stem: Why does a comet's tail always point away from the Sun?
options: The tail trails behind the comet along the path it has just travelled
The Sun's gravity pulls the tail out on the side facing the Sun
The tail is the shadow of the comet's icy core cast into space
Sunlight and the solar wind push its gas and dust away from the Sun
questions.explanation: As a comet nears the Sun its ice turns to gas, releasing dust, and the pressure of sunlight and the solar wind blows this material away from the Sun. So when the comet heads back out, its tail actually goes in front of it. The idea that the tail simply trails behind like smoke from a moving car is the common misconception.

questions.stem: A space rock burns up as a bright streak across the night sky, and one surviving piece lands on the Nullarbor Plain. What is the piece on the ground called?
options: A meteor
A meteoroid
A comet
A meteorite
questions.explanation: A meteoroid is the rock while it is still in space, a meteor is the streak of light as it burns through the atmosphere, and a meteorite is any piece that reaches the ground. The dry, flat Nullarbor is a good place to find meteorites because dark rocks stand out there.

questions.stem: What is a moon?
options: A natural satellite that orbits a planet
A small star that orbits close to a planet
A planet that has drifted away from its star
A rock orbiting the Sun between Mars and Jupiter
questions.explanation: A moon is a natural body that orbits a planet, as our Moon orbits Earth. A rock orbiting the Sun in the asteroid belt is an asteroid, not a moon, and moons do not make their own light the way stars do.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a star and a planet?
options: A star makes its own light; a planet only reflects light
A planet makes its own light; a star only reflects light
A star and a planet both make their own light by burning
A star reflects moonlight; a planet reflects sunlight
questions.explanation: Stars such as the Sun produce light by nuclear fusion in their cores. Planets do not produce visible light; we see them because they reflect sunlight, which is why Venus can outshine every star in the night sky despite making no light of its own.

questions.stem: The Southern Cross, or Crux, is an example of which kind of object?
options: A spiral galaxy
A dwarf planet
A planetary nebula
A constellation
questions.explanation: A constellation is a pattern of stars as seen from Earth, and the Southern Cross appears on the Australian flag. Its stars are at very different distances from us and only look grouped together from our viewpoint, unlike the stars of a galaxy, which are held together by gravity.

questions.stem: Mercury orbits the Sun in 88 days, while Neptune takes about 165 years. What best explains the difference?
options: Neptune is much heavier, and heavier planets always travel more slowly around the Sun
Neptune spins slowly on its axis, and slow spin drags its orbit to a crawl
Mercury is dragged along faster by the asteroid belt lying just beyond it
Neptune is much further away, so its orbit is far longer and it moves more slowly
questions.explanation: The further a planet is from the Sun, the longer the path it must travel and the weaker the Sun's gravity on it, so it moves more slowly. A planet's own mass does not set its orbital period — Jupiter is far heavier than Neptune but orbits in only about 12 years. The asteroid belt lies beyond Mars, nowhere near Mercury.

questions.stem: In Ptolemy's model of the universe, which body was at the centre?
options: The Sun
The Moon
Jupiter
Earth
questions.explanation: Ptolemy's geocentric model placed Earth at the centre, with the Moon, Sun, planets and stars moving around it. It matched everyday experience, since the Sun appears to cross our sky, and it was widely used for about 1400 years.

questions.stem: What change did Copernicus make to the model of the solar system in 1543?
options: He placed the Sun at the centre, with Earth orbiting it like the other planets
He showed that the planets travel in ellipses rather than in perfect circular paths
He discovered four moons orbiting Jupiter by looking through a telescope
He proved that Earth is round by measuring shadows in two different cities
questions.explanation: Copernicus proposed a heliocentric model with the Sun at the centre and Earth as one of several planets orbiting it. Ellipses came later from Kepler, and Jupiter's moons were discovered by Galileo in 1610. Measuring shadows to show Earth's curvature was done in ancient Greece by Eratosthenes.

questions.stem: Why was Galileo's discovery of moons orbiting Jupiter so important?
options: It proved that the planets move in elliptical orbits
It showed that Jupiter is a star rather than a planet
It proved that Earth's Moon broke away from Jupiter long ago
It showed that not every object in the sky orbits Earth
questions.explanation: In Ptolemy's model everything circled Earth, so moons circling Jupiter were direct evidence against it. Galileo's telescope observations did not reveal ellipses — that came from Kepler's analysis of Mars's motion — and Jupiter remained a planet.

questions.stem: Galileo observed that Venus shows a full set of phases, from crescent to nearly full. Why did this count against Ptolemy's Earth-centred model?
options: A full set of phases is only possible if Venus orbits the Sun
It showed that Venus makes its own light, just like a star
It showed that Venus has moons, which an Earth-centred model forbids
It showed that Venus is much larger than Earth and cannot orbit it
questions.explanation: In Ptolemy's model Venus always stayed between Earth and the Sun, so it could only ever appear as a crescent. Seeing Venus nearly full means it must sometimes pass behind the Sun, which happens only if it orbits the Sun. Phases come from reflected sunlight, which is evidence that Venus does not make its own light.

questions.stem: Kepler adjusted the Sun-centred model so that it matched careful measurements of where the planets appeared. What was his key change?
options: Earth sits at the centre after all, with the Sun orbiting it
Planets keep exactly the same speed all around their orbits
The stars are attached to a solid sphere that turns daily
Planets move in elliptical orbits, not perfect circles
questions.explanation: Copernicus kept perfect circles, so his model still did not quite match observations. Kepler showed that planets travel in ellipses with the Sun at one focus, and that they move faster when closer to the Sun, so their speed is not constant. This is an example of a model being modified rather than rejected when new evidence arrives.
